The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The English Beat – Mirror in the Bathroom (1980); Held Out Against Violence and Racism Through Music; Second Wave Ended ~1985
podcast.body: The English Beat, led by Dave Wakeling, were formed in the late 1970s and had their first hit with "Mirror in the Bathroom" (1980), a classic of the great ska revival. The second wave of ska — spanning roughly 1979 to 1985 — was vibrant and carried a hopeful message as a positive alternative to hard economic times and racial riots in Britain. By the mid-1980s, Jerry Dammers was broke and Two-Tone was falling apart under huge debt; despite efforts by the Clash, the Beat, and Bad Manners, the second wave ended around 1985. "Ska was a positive alternative to the hard economic times and the racial riots that were plaguing Britain in the early 1980s."

podcast.title: Ranking Roger's Death in 2019
podcast.body: Ranking Roger, a member of The English Beat, died in 2019. "Ranking Roger of the English Beat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In Memoriam of Those Lost in 2022

podcast.title: Advocacy for Inclusion and Anti-Racism
podcast.body: Like The Specials, The English Beat was committed to themes of inclusion and actively fighting racism through their music and message. "But like the specials, the English beat was all about inclusion and fighting racism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Birmingham Headquarters
podcast.body: The band was headquartered in Birmingham, a city known for its significant West Indian immigrant population. "They came on the scene just after the specials and were headquartered in Birmingham, another city of choice for plenty of West Indian immigrants."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Ska Punk
podcast.body: The English Beat, along with The Specials, played a vital role in shaping the post-punk world and are considered instrumental in the development of Ska punk. "It weren't for bands like the beat and the specials. Would we have all the Scott punk that we have today?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jamaican Influence from Members
podcast.body: Vocalist Ranking Roger and saxophonist Saxa, both black members of the band, infused their music with strong Jamaican influences. "Vocalist ranking Roger and saxophone as saxo, both of whom are black, added plenty of Jamaican influence to the music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Motown Influence and Genre Fusion
podcast.body: The band's influences extended to Motown music, demonstrating a broader scope than just Ska. They uniquely applied Ska principles to a Motown groove. "everybody in the band was a big fan of Motown. They even covered this hit by Smoky Robinson in the Miracles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: North American Importation by Seymour Stein
podcast.body: The English Beat were among the "unknown English bands" that legendary record executive Seymour Stein, founder of Sire Records, imported into North America, contributing to their rise in popularity. "He's the guy that imported unknown English bands like The Smiths and The Pretenders and The English Beat into North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Post-Punk Interracial Ska Band
podcast.body: The English Beat emerged after The Specials as another prominent post-punk interracial Ska band, based in Birmingham. "And for talking about post-punk interracial Scott bands, we have to mention the English beat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radio Discovery in Brandon, Manitoba
podcast.body: The speaker learned about The English Beat while working at KX96 in Brandon, Manitoba, a station known for its eclectic mix of music in 1983. "So that's where I learned a little bit about the English beat and the specials and a few other artists that we played."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Representative New Wave and 2 Tone Artist
podcast.body: English Beat was cited as part of the "new Scott Seen," a subgenre within the expansive New Wave umbrella. This reference underscores their role in the 2 Tone movement and its classification within the broader New Wave context. "There was Power Pop, which could include everyone from Elvis Costello to Tom Petty, a new Scott Seen, a specials English beat and so on, and all of the flavors of Technopop, all those groups who threw away their guitars and favor of synthesizers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Saxa's Ska Pedigree
podcast.body: Saxa, the band's saxophonist, had previously played with legendary Ska artists like Prince Buster and Desmond Dekker, bringing deep genre knowledge to The English Beat. "saxo had played with Scott Giants like Prince Buster and Desmond Decker in the early days, so this guy really knew what he was doing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Second Wave Ska Band
podcast.body: The English Beat is mentioned as a British group associated with the "Two Tone" sound, characteristic of the "second wave" of ska in the late 1970s and early 1980s. "Second wave Skop was what we heard from two tone bands, like the Specials, and British groups like Madness and the English beats in the late 70s and early 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Selling Blank Cassettes at Shows
podcast.body: The band sold blank cassettes at their merchandise table during their shows, actively encouraging fans to bootleg the performances and copy their records. This action directly contradicted the music industry's "Home Taping Is Killing Music" campaign. `"The English beat sold blank cassettes at their merch table at their shows, in hopes that fans would bootleg the show and copy their records."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1
